title: 2025 Status Report on Hunger in Rhode Island ("Historic Highs")
publication_date: 2026-01-27 (scheduled release date; page itself is undated)
abstract: Annual hunger report, delayed from Thanksgiving to reflect the fall 2025 federal shutdown. Says the shutdown exposed how fragile food security is for tens of thousands of Rhode Islanders.
key_takeaways: Food Bank network has 137 member agencies. Search coverage of the report cites 102,000+ people needing help during the SNAP lapse (a record) and about 1 in 3 families food insecure before the shutdown. Recommends more state hunger-relief funding, a food insecurity task force, and preparing for SNAP changes. Full numbers are in the PDF, which I could not read.
verification: Landing page read; figures in this row come from search summaries, not the PDF

title: Extra SNAP benefits coming to an end next month
abstract: Explains that federal SNAP Emergency Allotments created in March 2020 are ending, reducing household grocery money from March 1, 2023.
key_takeaways: Households got either the max benefit for their size or an extra $95/month. Rhode Island's last expanded benefit was issued Feb 1, 2023. RI advised recipients to update income and household info, which could raise regular benefits.

title: Rep. Morales helps secure $3 million investment for the Rhode Island Community Food Bank
publisher_author: Rhode Island General Assembly press release
abstract: Legislative press release on the FY24 state budget appropriation for the Food Bank, in response to the end of pandemic SNAP boosts.
key_takeaways: FY24 budget gave the Food Bank $3 million. Emergency SNAP cuts in March 2023 affected 80,000+ RI households. People served at pantries and meal sites rose from 66,000 (Feb 2023) to 79,000 (Mar 2023), +20%. Food insecurity was more than 3x pre-pandemic levels.

title: Report: Too many Rhode Islanders are going hungry
abstract: Coverage of the Food Bank's 2023 Status Report on Hunger.
key_takeaways: 77,000+ people/month used pantries Jan-Sep 2023, up 30%+ from 2022 (about 52,000 pre-COVID). 29% of all households and 38% of households with children food insecure. Average RI household lost $155/month when emergency SNAP ended. Food Bank asked for state funding to rise from $550,000 to $1 million and for free school meals for all.

title: Food bank says more Rhode Island families can't afford food
abstract: AP coverage of the Food Bank's 2022 annual hunger report.
key_takeaways: 31% of surveyed households could not afford adequate food (18.4% in 2021, 25.2% in 2020, 9.1% in 2017-19). Food prices up 13% in a year. Pantries served about 63,000 residents/month, about 10,000 more than in 2021. Food insecurity was 3x its pre-pandemic level.

title: 2024 RI Life Index shows Rhode Islanders perceive continuing challenges in housing, cost of living and food security
publisher_author: Brown University School of Public Health / BCBSRI
abstract: Press release for the sixth RI Life Index, a statewide survey of 1,946 adults.
key_takeaways: Access to nutritious food scored 64/100, down 2 points from 2023 and 9 from 2021. Latino respondents' food security did not rebound to 2020-22 levels.

title: Nearly 2 in 5 R.I. households are food insecure, new report says
abstract: Coverage of the Food Bank's 2024 report, based on RI Life Index data collected March-April 2024.
key_takeaways: 38% food insecure, up from 29% in 2023 and the highest during the pandemic era. By group: Latino 55%, Black 47%, Asian/Native American/multiracial 47%, white 33%. 84,400 people/month served Jan-Sep 2024 (+9%). Low-income residents miss 42.2M+ meals/year. 90,500 RI households on SNAP. State Food Bank funding rose to $800,000 in FY25.

title: More than a third of Rhode Islanders are facing food insecurity, according to a new survey
abstract: Radio news report on the 2024 RI Life Index food insecurity result, released by the Food Bank.
key_takeaways: 38% of households food insecure, a five-year high and up 111% from 18% in 2021. Latino 55%, Black 47%, white 33%. About 2,000 randomly selected adults surveyed by phone. Definition: worrying about or lacking money for food at least some of the time. Pantries are seeing first-time users.

title: Assessing Hunger in Rhode Island: 2025 Updates and the Rhode Island Community Food Bank's Spring Initiatives
publication_date: 2025-03 (approximate; page is undated, refers to 'as of March 2025')
abstract: Food Bank summary of state hunger data, disparities, state funding and the SNAP produce incentive, plus spring events.
key_takeaways: About 38% of households food insecure. 33% white, 47% Black, 55% Latino, 47% other. 84,400 people/month served in 2024 (+9%). State allotment rose from $550,000 (FY24) to $800,000 (FY25). Eat Well, Be Well pays 50 cents back per $1 of produce, up to $25/month.

title: SNAP State Fact Sheet: Rhode Island
publication_date: 2025-02/03 (file name dated 022525; related technical notes created 2025-05-16)
abstract: Single-state fact sheet on SNAP participation and benefits.
key_takeaways: SNAP helps 136,179 people in Rhode Island. Across 2019-2023, an average of 79% of RI SNAP households included a worker.

title: SNAP shutdown leaves 145,000 Rhode Islanders facing food insecurity as Nov. 1 deadline looms
abstract: Reports that USDA would not send November 2025 SNAP funds because of the federal shutdown.
key_takeaways: About 145,000 RI residents receive SNAP; RI gets about $29M/month. Average benefit $199/month. Gov. McKee declared a state of emergency and proposed shifting $6M to prevent hunger. AG Neronha joined a multistate suit. Newport pantry and hot-meal use rose.

title: Thousands in New England to lose SNAP eligibility as new federal requirements take effect
abstract: Explains how the One Big Beautiful Bill Act's SNAP changes take effect Nov 1, 2025.
key_takeaways: About 2,300 RI households permanently lose SNAP; 5,300 cases become subject to work requirements and 4,000 lose exemptions. Work age limit rises from 54 to 64. RI payment error rate 12.29% in FY24 vs 10.93% national; states above 6% pay a share of benefits from FY2028.

title: 'One Big Beautiful Bill Act' threatens Medicaid coverage, SNAP benefits for thousands in R.I., state's analysis finds
abstract: Coverage of the state's own analysis of the federal law's effect on RI.
key_takeaways: At least 2,300 households lose SNAP entirely (asylum seekers, trafficking and domestic violence survivors, other humanitarian entrants). Hundreds more see reduced benefits. Pantries and resettlement agencies expect more demand. State faces about a $300M FY27 deficit.

title: 5 things to know about SNAP in Rhode Island
abstract: Explainer on RI SNAP enrollment, local variation, benefit levels, federal changes and food insecurity.
key_takeaways: About 138,000 people (13%) on SNAP, up from about 76,000 in 2005. Woonsocket 26%, Providence 23%, Central Falls 22%, Pawtucket 20%; under 3% in Jamestown, Barrington, New Shoreham. Max benefit $298/month for one person, $975 for a family of four. Federal changes could cost RI $51M/year from 2027. Food Bank serves 89,000/month vs about 50,000 pre-pandemic.

title: SNAP data by RI county, State House districts & State Senate districts
abstract: County and legislative-district SNAP participation estimates for RI.
key_takeaways: Over 90,000 households and about 144,000 people rely on SNAP. Built from USDA FY2024 average monthly participation and 2023 ACS 5-year estimates (DP03), rounded to the nearest 100.

title: Rhode Island Community Food Bank delays release of its annual hunger report
publisher_author: Rhode Island Current (Christopher Shea), via Providence Business News
abstract: Explains the Food Bank's decision to push its 2025 report to January 27, 2026 so it captures the shutdown's effect.
key_takeaways: Shutdown disrupted SNAP for 145,000 Rhode Islanders. Pantries served about 100,000 in October 2025 vs 84,400/month the year before. Refugees and other immigrants lose SNAP access starting Feb 1, 2026. The usual spring RI Life Index survey would miss the fall spike.

title: Nation's first state-level SNAP fresh produce incentive program shows promise, room to grow
publisher_author: Brown University School of Public Health
abstract: Evaluation of Rhode Island's Eat Well, Be Well program (launched January 2024), comparing 725 SNAP recipients in RI and Connecticut.
key_takeaways: Program returns $0.50 per $1 on fresh produce, up to $25/month. Modest, non-significant increases in produce intake. About 1 in 3 could describe the program; about 1 in 4 used it. Only Stop & Shop and Walmart participated at launch, limiting access for shoppers who use other stores and who face transportation barriers.

title: Rhode Islanders report challenges with cost of living, access to affordable housing and nutritious food
abstract: Results of the seventh RI Life Index (BCBSRI and Brown SPH), a random-digit-dial survey of 2,117 adults plus a panel.
key_takeaways: 44% of RI Voices panel respondents experienced household food insecurity in the past year (described as record-high). Overall well-being score 57/100, the lowest on record. Cost of living scored 21 and affordable housing 30. Grocery prices changed how people shop.

title: Why Rhode Island can't afford to lose the race to reduce its SNAP error rate
publisher_author: Rhode Island Current (Nancy Lavin), via Boston Globe
abstract: Reports on RI's effort to cut its SNAP payment error rate before the federal cost-share begins Oct 1, 2027.
key_takeaways: Error rate 12.3% in FY24 (national 10.9%); preliminary 7.6%. Missing the limit could cost RI up to $100M/year (up to 15% of program cost). About 140,000 residents on SNAP; participation fell 7% from July to December 2025. DHS had 88 vacancies of 779 positions. Work requirements from March 1 expected to affect 9,000 people. Governor proposes doubling Food Bank funding to $2M.

title: 2026 Rhode Island KIDS COUNT Factbook: SNAP Benefits
abstract: Factbook indicator page on children receiving SNAP.
key_takeaways: Children on SNAP fell 31% over a decade, from just over 60,000 (2016) to about 42,000 (2025). In October 2025, 67% of SNAP households had gross income below the federal poverty level. Child hunger falls by about one third after 6 months of SNAP.

title: Federal data gaps aside, poverty on the rise as R.I. families struggle to meet basic living expenses
publisher_author: Rhode Island Current (Alexander Castro), via Boston Globe
abstract: Coverage of the 2026 KIDS COUNT Factbook, including USDA's end of its food security report.
key_takeaways: Child poverty 16.3% (2024 data), up from 13.3%. Children on SNAP down 31% in 10 years. USDA ended its Household Food Security Report; the final edition came out Oct 2025. Single parent with two young children needs about $83,239/year. 1,994 students identified as homeless in 2024-25, up 36% since 2021-22.

title: SNAP Update
abstract: Advocacy resource on SNAP losses after the June 1, 2026 enforcement of federal work rules.
key_takeaways: 5,000 more Rhode Islanders lost SNAP on June 1 under H.R.1. Benefits can be restored if work went unreported, if the person now meets 20 hrs/week or 80 hrs/month, or if an exemption applies. Appeals go through DHS.

title: 2026 Rhode Island KIDS COUNT Factbook: School Meals
abstract: Factbook indicator page on school breakfast and lunch participation and free-meal policy.
key_takeaways: 1 in 7 (15%) households with children were food insecure in 2021-2023. Since 2024-25, children who qualified for reduced-price meals get free meals ($813,000 for about 6,500 students). Sept 2025: 32,069 children in School Breakfast and 68,872 in School Lunch. SUN Bucks launched in 2025 at $120 per child.

title: Department of Human Services FY 2027 budget presentation
abstract: House Finance subcommittee staff analysis of the Governor's FY27 DHS budget, including SNAP.
key_takeaways: FY26 SNAP appropriation $424.9M serving about 145,000 people. Federal admin match drops from 50% to 25% on Oct 1, 2026, with about $9.3M extra state cost in FY27. Governor proposes error-rate initiatives with 29 positions. Benefit cost-sharing starts Oct 1, 2027.

title: Food Justice Report (Rhode Island College Food Justice Project)
abstract: Student report reviewing food justice, food deserts and food insecurity in RI, focused on Providence, Olneyville, South Providence and Woonsocket.
key_takeaways: Argues access problems persist south and west of I-95. Suggests 'grocery gap' may fit non-urban areas like West Warwick better than 'food desert'.
